body:
How a tropical cyclone develops

A tropical cyclone is an organised rotating weather system with a low-pressure centre, strong winds and deep convective clouds. It develops over warm tropical or subtropical seas when atmospheric conditions support sustained rising motion and organised circulation.

Warm ocean water supplies heat and moisture through evaporation. Moist air rises and cools, causing water vapour to condense into cloud droplets. Condensation releases latent heat, which helps sustain rising air and the low-pressure system. Surrounding air moves towards the lower-pressure region, and Earth's rotation helps organise the circulation.

Several conditions favour tropical cyclone formation, including sufficiently warm ocean water, available moisture, an existing atmospheric disturbance and wind conditions that allow the storm to remain organised. A cyclone does not form merely because the sea is warm; the other atmospheric conditions must also be favourable.

Rotation and the eye

Because of the Coriolis effect, cyclonic circulation is generally anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere. The Coriolis effect is very weak near the equator, which is one reason tropical cyclones rarely form extremely close to it.

In a well-developed intense tropical cyclone, the central eye may have relatively calm conditions. Around it lies the eyewall, containing some of the strongest winds and most intense rainfall. Rainbands extend outward from the central circulation.

A calm eye does not mean that the cyclone has ended. Dangerous eyewall conditions can return as the storm continues to move.

Three distinct sources of cyclone damage

Strong winds

High winds can damage roofs, poorly secured structures, trees, electricity lines, communication networks and boats. Flying debris creates additional danger. The severity of damage depends on wind speed, exposure and the strength of structures and their connections.

Storm surge

Storm surge is the abnormal rise of sea level caused by a storm above the water level predicted from the ordinary astronomical tide. The most important cause is strong wind pushing seawater towards the coast; low atmospheric pressure also contributes.

The impact of storm surge depends on the storm's strength, size, movement and angle of approach, as well as the shape of the coastline and the depth of nearby water. Low-lying coasts, bays and estuaries may experience particularly severe inundation. A broad, shallow continental shelf can favour large storm surges under suitable storm conditions.

Heavy rainfall

Cyclones can produce intense or prolonged rainfall, causing flooding, waterlogging, river overflow and disruption of transport and essential services. Serious rainfall-related damage may occur well inland after the cyclone crosses the coast. A place outside the area of the strongest winds can still face dangerous flooding.

Storm surge, storm tide and tsunami

Astronomical tide is the regular sea-level variation caused chiefly by the gravitational effects of the Moon and Sun. Storm surge is the storm-produced rise above the predicted astronomical tide. Storm tide is the resulting water level when the astronomical tide and storm surge combine.

A dangerous storm surge arriving around high tide can produce a higher total coastal water level than a similar surge occurring around low tide. This is why coastal-flood warnings may refer to surge height above astronomical tide.

A tsunami differs fundamentally because its initiating mechanism is sudden water displacement, commonly associated with an undersea earthquake. A cyclone's strong winds do not convert its storm surge into a tsunami.

Cyclones and the Indian coastline

Tropical cyclones occur over both the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea. India's eastern coast has historically experienced greater cyclone frequency, but the western coast is also exposed. Gujarat's Saurashtra and Kutch coastlines, fishing communities, ports, coastal industries and low-lying settlements require cyclone and storm-surge preparedness.

Prelims focus

  • A tropical cyclone is an organised rotating low-pressure system.
  • Latent heat released during condensation helps sustain tropical cyclones.
  • Cyclonic rotation in the Northern Hemisphere is generally anticlockwise.
  • The eyewall generally contains the most intense winds around a developed cyclone's eye.
  • Storm tide combines astronomical tide and storm surge.
  • Trap: A cyclone can cause serious inland flooding even far from its strongest coastal winds.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 8, Winds, Storms and Cyclones, printed pp. 80–91, 2018–19 printing; India Meteorological Department, Cyclone Warning in India: Standard Operation Procedure, March 2021, Chapter 1; National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, What Is Storm Surge?, sections on storm surge and storm tide; Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority, Gujarat State Disaster Management Plan 2020–21, Volume 2, Chapter 2, Action Plan for Cyclone. Official sources consulted 2 November 2026.]

title: Tropical Cyclone Formation, Structure and the Three Major Hazards

body:
How India classifies cyclonic disturbances

The India Meteorological Department (IMD) classifies cyclonic disturbances over the North Indian Ocean using their maximum sustained surface wind speed. The standard classification uses a 3-minute sustained-wind averaging period. This is different from an instantaneous wind gust.

ClassificationMaximum sustained wind (km/h)
Depression31–49
Deep depression50–61
Cyclonic storm62–88
Severe cyclonic storm89–117
Very severe cyclonic storm118–166
Extremely severe cyclonic storm167–221
Super cyclonic storm222 or more

A tropical disturbance becomes a cyclonic storm under this classification when its maximum sustained wind reaches the cyclonic-storm category. Stronger categories indicate greater maximum sustained winds, but they do not alone determine every local impact. Rainfall, storm surge, storm size, track and local vulnerability are also important.

How cyclones are monitored and forecast

Modern cyclone forecasting combines observations from several sources with numerical weather-prediction models:

  • Meteorological satellites observe cloud organisation, movement and other features over large ocean areas.
  • Doppler weather radar provides detailed observations of precipitation and storm structure where the cyclone is within radar coverage.
  • Ocean observations and weather stations provide supporting information on atmospheric and marine conditions.
  • Numerical models estimate possible movement, intensification, landfall and associated hazards.

A track forecast estimates where the cyclone may travel. An intensity forecast estimates how strong it may become. A forecast of landfall concerns when and where the storm's centre is expected to cross the coast. Dangerous weather may begin before the centre makes landfall and may affect places outside the precise landfall point.

IMD's 4-stage warning system

For cyclones approaching India's coast under the standard system, IMD issues progressively more specific bulletins to support government and public preparedness.

StageUsual lead timePurpose
Pre-cyclone watch72 hours before adverse weatherIndicate possible cyclone development and threatened coastal areas
Cyclone alert48 hours before adverse weatherProvide developing information on storm location, intensity and likely coastal impacts
Cyclone warning24 hours before adverse weatherSpecify expected landfall and hazards such as wind, rain and storm surge
Post-landfall outlook12 hours before expected landfallDescribe likely movement and adverse weather over interior areas after landfall

Important timing distinction: The 72-hour, 48-hour and 24-hour stages are referenced to the expected commencement of adverse weather; the 12-hour post-landfall outlook is referenced to expected landfall.

The warning stages are a standard arrangement, not a guarantee that all 4 bulletins will always appear at those exact intervals. A cyclone that forms close to the coast or intensifies rapidly may require warnings to be issued with shorter lead times or without every earlier stage.

From forecast to protective action

IMD provides the scientific forecasts and meteorological warnings. State and district authorities use this information to organise public communication, warnings to fishing communities, shelters and evacuation where necessary. Local administrations, village institutions and community volunteers are important for last-mile delivery of instructions.

Warnings must be interpreted as developing assessments, not promises of a particular outcome. A forecast track may shift as new observations become available. Households should follow the latest verified bulletin and instructions rather than relying on an older prediction.

Prelims focus

  • A cyclonic storm has maximum sustained winds of 62–88 km/h under IMD's North Indian Ocean classification.
  • A severe cyclonic storm has maximum sustained winds of 89–117 km/h.
  • A super cyclonic storm has maximum sustained winds of 222 km/h or more.
  • IMD's standard stages are pre-cyclone watch, cyclone alert, cyclone warning and post-landfall outlook.
  • The standard lead times are 72, 48, 24 and 12 hours, with different reference points for the last stage.
  • Trap: Maximum sustained wind speed is not the same as a short wind gust.

[Sources: India Meteorological Department, Frequently Asked Questions on Tropical Cyclones, 26 April 2023, sections on wind-based classification and intensity; India Meteorological Department, Cyclone Warning in India: Standard Operation Procedure, March 2021, Section 6.5.1, Four Stage Warning Bulletin; India Meteorological Department, Regional Specialised Meteorological Centre New Delhi, Four Stage Warning and Bulletin Products, sections on warning stages and dissemination. Official sources consulted 2 November 2026.]

body:
Preparedness before a cyclone approaches

Cyclone risk reduction requires attention to strong winds, coastal inundation and rainfall-related flooding together. Focusing only on the cyclone's maximum wind speed can leave people unprepared for storm surge and freshwater flooding.

When a cyclone threatens a coastal district, households should follow official forecasts and local evacuation instructions. Basic preparedness includes storing safe drinking water, securing essential medicines and documents, keeping communication devices usable and identifying the safest available shelter.

Fishing communities should follow official restrictions on going to sea. Boats, fishing equipment, livestock and other movable property may need protection or relocation when this can be done safely and before conditions become dangerous. People should not delay necessary evacuation merely to protect possessions.

Evacuation and cyclone shelters

A cyclone shelter is a designated safer refuge for people exposed to the approaching storm. Its location, structural safety, accessibility and capacity matter. In storm-surge-prone areas, appropriate elevation and distance from expected inundation are especially important.

Evacuation is most effective when it occurs before dangerous wind, rain or coastal flooding makes travel unsafe. A person ordered to evacuate should use the specified route and shelter rather than remaining in a vulnerable house because the immediate weather still appears calm.

Shelter arrangements should consider children, pregnant women, older persons, persons with disabilities and people requiring assistance. Safe drinking water, sanitation, basic health support and accessible information are important for maintaining safety and dignity.

Resilient housing and infrastructure

Reducing cyclone damage requires safer buildings and reliable essential services. Measures include appropriate structural design for local wind hazards, secure roof connections, protection of vulnerable openings and avoidance of construction in highly exposed locations where safer options exist. Technical design must follow applicable requirements and professional assessment.

Hospitals, schools, electricity infrastructure, water-supply systems, roads, communication networks and ports require continuity and recovery planning. A damaged road can delay access to a shelter, while damaged electricity or water infrastructure may create serious post-cyclone difficulties even after the strongest winds have passed.

Coastal planning may also conserve mangroves, dunes and other suitable ecosystems that reduce some erosion and wave effects. These measures complement, rather than replace, safe building practices and evacuation.

Public precautions during and after the storm

  • Stay in the designated safe shelter until local authorities advise that conditions are safe.
  • Avoid standing floodwater, submerged roads and coastal areas affected by surge.
  • Do not approach fallen electrical lines or touch wet electrical equipment.
  • Use safe drinking water and follow public-health instructions when supplies may be contaminated.
  • Do not assume the danger has ended because winds temporarily become lighter.
  • Follow verified official information rather than rumours or unconfirmed messages.

Livelihood recovery is part of disaster recovery

After a cyclone, immediate relief addresses urgent shelter, food, drinking water and health needs. Recovery then seeks to restore homes, roads, utilities, public facilities and economic activities.

Fishing livelihoods may be affected by damaged boats, nets, landing centres and cold-chain or market facilities. Agriculture may suffer crop damage, waterlogging, damaged irrigation facilities or saltwater intrusion. Small traders and wage workers may lose income when roads, electricity and markets remain disrupted.

Livelihood recovery may therefore require restoration of productive assets, market access and basic services, together with suitable financial and social support. Reconstruction should reduce the risk of repeating the same losses in a future cyclone.

Gujarat example: Cyclone Biparjoy in June 2023

Very Severe Cyclonic Storm Biparjoy approached the Saurashtra and Kutch coast in June 2023. In an official bulletin issued on 15 June 2023, IMD forecast landfall near Jakhau Port and warned of strong winds and coastal inundation.

That bulletin forecast a storm surge of 2–3 metres above the astronomical tide in vulnerable low-lying coastal areas. This was a forecast issued at that time, not a claim that every location subsequently experienced the same measured rise. The distinction is important: a forecast hazard value must not automatically be presented as an observed result.

The event illustrates Gujarat's exposure to Arabian Sea cyclones and the practical importance of wind, rainfall, tide and coastal-vulnerability information being used together in evacuation and shelter decisions.

Prelims focus

  • Cyclone preparedness must address wind, storm surge and heavy rain together.
  • Evacuation should be completed before routes become unsafe.
  • Cyclone shelters should be structurally safe and appropriately located for local hazards.
  • Floodwater and fallen electrical lines remain dangerous after winds weaken.
  • Biparjoy threatened the Saurashtra and Kutch coast in June 2023.
  • Trap: A forecast storm-surge height is not necessarily the later observed height.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 8, Winds, Storms and Cyclones, printed pp. 88–92, 2018–19 printing; Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority, Gujarat State Disaster Management Plan 2020–21, Volume 2, Chapter 2, Action Plan for Cyclone; India Meteorological Department, Hourly Update on Very Severe Cyclonic Storm Biparjoy, Bulletin No. 06, issued 15 June 2023 at 1715 IST, p. 1, landfall and forecast storm-surge entries; National Disaster Management Authority, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Cyclones, 2008, chapters on preparedness, mitigation and response. Official sources consulted 2 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Early evacuation allows coastal households to reach safer shelter before cyclone conditions become dangerous.

title: Cyclone and Storm-Surge Preparedness, Safer Infrastructure and Livelihood Recovery
